Almost the same.

Two beginnings can differ by almost nothing and still become very different. This is the Lorenz system: three simple differential equations producing a path that never quite repeats. Change the conditions. Watch what happens.

A moving diagram of the Lorenz attractor.LORENZ SYSTEM / PROJECTION OF 3D MOTION
One trajectory. Try parallel universes to compare two nearly identical beginnings.

What are you seeing?

Both trajectories obey the same equations. Only the initial x-coordinate differs. Their separation is an illustration of sensitivity to initial conditions—not a literal multiverse, and not proof that tiny differences always produce dramatically different outcomes.

At ρ = 28, the classic Lorenz parameters produce a chaotic attractor. At other values, behavior can change. The lines show a moving window of recent positions, projected from three dimensions onto a flat screen.

Equations: dx/dt = 10(y − x), dy/dt = x(ρ − z) − y, dz/dt = xy − (8/3)z. Integrated numerically with fourth-order Runge–Kutta. Everything runs locally in your browser.

This is a playful mathematical model, not a simulation of alternate human lives.
